vignette:
Robert is seventy-one years old, a lifelong bachelor who still works part-time from a cramped home office for a regional insurance firm. He lives alone in a two-bedroom bungalow on a quiet street, his days measured out in policy renewals, claim forms, and the precise arrangement of pens on his desk. He has been doing this work for forty-three years, and he is very good at it. His clients appreciate his thoroughness, though they sometimes find him distant.

He does not like to be touched without warning. When a colleague once clapped him on the shoulder at an office party, Robert flinched and dropped a cup of coffee. He apologized immediately, said he must be getting old. But the truth is that he has been flinching for sixty-five years, ever since his mother's hand came down on his back, his face, his bare legs, for reasons he could never predict. She was his caregiver after his father left, and she was tired, overwhelmed, and angry in ways that had nothing to do with a child's mistakes. Robert learned early that safety meant staying still, staying quiet, and watching for the shift in her voice that meant a blow was coming.

The worst memory comes back to him in fragments, never the whole picture. He is six years old and has accidentally spilled a glass of milk on the kitchen floor. She grabs him by the arm, drags him to the bathroom, and holds his head under the faucet while the cold water runs. He cannot breathe. He is not crying anymore because crying made it worse. He remembers the tile pattern, the smell of soap, the way his teeth chattered long after she let him go. That night she told him he was a bad boy and that she only did these things because she loved him. He believed her for a long time.

In school, he was the boy who never raised his hand. He sat at the back, finished his work silently, and left the moment the bell rang. He made no close friends. He learned that being invisible was safer. As an adult, he gravitated to insurance because it was orderly: risk could be calculated, outcomes predicted, payments scheduled. There were no surprises in a policy. He became an expert at reading fine print, at spotting the hidden clauses that might cause a client trouble later. He prided himself on being thorough. His coworkers said he was meticulous, but they did not see how he read every document three times, or how he could not sleep the night before a difficult meeting, or how he kept a small led flashlight in his nightstand drawer in case the power went out.

Robert has never married. He came close once, in his thirties, to a woman named Helen who was kind and patient. But after a few months, she touched his arm unexpectedly while he was cooking, and he turned and shoved her away. He did not mean to, he said. He apologized over and over. She left a week later. He understood. He still writes her a Christmas card every year, always the same one: a generic snow scene, signed "Best wishes, Robert." He never sends it.

Now, at seventy-one, his life is small and predictable. He wakes at six, makes toast and black coffee, and sits at his desk by seven. He avoids the news, especially stories about children or families. He changes the channel if a movie shows a parent yelling. He has not spoken to his mother since he moved out at eighteen. She died ten years ago, alone in a nursing home, and he did not attend the funeral. He told himself it was because he was busy with work. But the truth is that he still feels six years old sometimes, cold and wet and waiting for the next blow. He does not know how to stop feeling that.

His PCL-5 scores-the ones his therapist asked him to fill out after his doctor referred him-add up to 39. That number means something moderate, something not yet overwhelming, but Robert does not think of himself as having a diagnosis. He thinks of himself as someone who has made it through, day after day, by staying very still.
